accuracy.evidence: Sun positions are not drawn by eye: sunAt() uses sin(alt) = sin(lat)sin(dec) + cos(lat)cos(dec)cos(H) with H = 15° per hour from solar noon and the matching azimuth formula, for 51.5° N. Checked in Python: March gives 18.1° at 8 am (shadow 3.05 m for a 1 m stick), 26.1° at 9 am (2.04 m), 32.6° at 10 am (1.56 m), 38.5° at noon (1.26 m); June noon 61.9° (0.53 m), December noon 15.1° (3.71 m). The adult text quotes these rounded and says solar midday is near 12 noon GMT and near 1 pm BST. Morning shadows are described as west or north-west because at 8.30 am in March the sun's bearing is about 121°, so the shadow points about 301°. Practice items use the symmetry about solar noon and the fact that shadow length scales with height for the same sun angle.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented shadow misconceptions from primary science research (Nuffield/SPACE and NGSS 5-ESS1-2 guidance): the shadow points towards the sun (prediction 1, claim 3, challenge 'toward', m8, and a feedback message when the sun is placed next to the flag), the shadow is longest at midday when the sun is strongest (claim 2, prediction 3, challenge 'longnoon', p4), shadows are the same all day (prediction 2 option, challenge 'same'), the sun moves round the Earth (claim 4, challenge 'sunmoves', p5) and the midday shadow is the same all year (prediction 4, claim 5, challenge 'season', m6).

lab_distinct.evidence: The lab is built on this topic's own model: a computed sun path for a real latitude driving a top-down shadow (direction) and a side view where one sunlight ray grazes the top of the stick (length), a time scrubber that plots the real shadow lengths on a chart and leaves the tip trail, reading the hour from a shadow, and the midday sun in three months from the declination. flagshadow (lesson 343, ages 4-5) is a torch and a teddy; flagshine is sunlight warming surfaces. The lab_distinct gate keeps flag_sunpath.js under 30% similar to every other flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner discovers each rule by acting: the flag is only reached when the sun is put on the opposite side, and putting the sun beside the flag gives a message naming the slip; the side view's readout shows 2.0 m at 27°, 1.0 m at 45° and 0.5 m at 63°, so higher sun means shorter shadow; the five plotted points (3.1, 1.6, 1.3, 1.6, 3.1 m) form the U on the chart while the grey tip dots trace across the north side; the month bars show 0.5, 1.3 and 3.7 m at midday. The text then confirms what they found.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab disproves: 'The sun is in the east, which way does the shadow point?' (tempting: towards the sun; the first flag needs the sun in the east to send the shadow west), 'The sun climbs higher, what happens to the shadow?' (tempting: longer; the readout shrinks), 'When will the shadow be shortest?' (tempting: 8 am; the chart's lowest point is noon) and 'When is the midday shadow longest?' (tempting: June or same all year; the December bar is 7 times the June bar). Each completion message reveals the learner's own prediction.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating challenge questions with two tagged wrong answers each and nine distinct messages in SUNP.SLIP: toward (shadows point away from the sun), south (morning sun is east so shadow goes west), longnoon (a low sun makes a long shadow), same (shadows change as the sun's height changes), lowshort (lower sun, longer shadow, with the torch picture), time (midday sun is due south so the shadow points north), sunmoves (the Earth spins), season (June high, December low) and other. The read-the-shadow scene also gives three reasoned messages from the shadow's direction.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences and everyday words (blocks the light, skims past the top, dark patch) and pass the learner readability limit in validate_lessons; adult paragraphs name the NGSS and Year 5 statements and key words and pass the adult limit. Canvas labels are dark text on white pills over pale sky and grass, and every pill shrinks to fit at 390 px (checked on iPhone 13 screenshots in dark theme and desktop in light).

no_filler.evidence: Each kid paragraph teaches one idea: how a shadow forms and points away, the Earth's spin and the sun's apparent path, sun height and shadow length, and the U-shaped chart with the winter midday shadow. Adult paragraphs give the standards, the physics with real figures for London, four named mistakes and what the lab does. The content gate found no filler phrases and under 12% overlap with every lesson, including 343 and 706.

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 (dark) and desktop (light) screenshots of every step at rest, part-way through Show me and finished, plus a wrong challenge answer: the compass ring and flag fit inside the canvas with N, E, S, W readable; the side view keeps the sun inside the sky and the 0-3 m ruler on screen at 15°; the day scene fits the top-down shadow with the chart below it and labels 8 am to 4 pm readable; the month bars and three answer boxes fit; buttons under the canvas wrap as 44 px targets.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a labelled button twin: move the sun towards east or west in 22.5° steps (all three flag positions reachable), sun lower or higher in 3° steps (27°, 45° and 63° reachable from 36°), 1 hour earlier or later (every plotted time reachable from 9 am), Morning, Midday and Afternoon, three month buttons, and Right or Wrong. Every change updates the canvas aria-label with the sun's position and the shadow's length and direction, results go through c.say, and challenge feedback is a polite live region. The walk gate's axe run is clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.

Department for Education (2013) Science programmes of study: key stages 1 and 2, Year 3 Light and Year 5 Earth and space (the Earth's rotation and the apparent movement of the sun across the sky)
Standard solar position formulas (NOAA Solar Calculator method): solar altitude and azimuth from latitude, declination and hour angle; declination ±23.44° at the solstices
